Renal ultrasound and referral to nephrology
questions.explain: Is it real, is it big? Start with urinalysis, confirm on first-morning urine (excludes orthostatic/transient) and quantify with a protein:creatinine ratio. Febrile illness commonly causes transient proteinuria.
questions.note: Start with urinalysis; confirm on first-morning urine; quantify with protein:creatinine ratio.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy has periorbital swelling for a week, now with ankle oedema. Urine shows 4+ protein, no blood; albumin is 16 g/L, BP and complement are normal. What is the most likely underlying histology?
questions.explain: Nephrotic syndrome aged 1-10 without haematuria, hypertension or low complement is minimal change disease in ~90%. Membranous is an adult disease; PSGN is nephritic with low C3.
questions.note: Nephrotic age 1-10 → minimal change disease (~90%).

questions.stem: A 4-year-old has typical nephrotic syndrome: heavy proteinuria, albumin 18 g/L, oedema, normal BP, normal renal function and normal complement. What is the most appropriate initial management?
options: Renal biopsy before starting any treatment
questions.explain: Typical nephrotic syndrome aged 1-10 is presumed minimal change and treated with steroids without biopsy; biopsy is for atypical features (age <1 or >10, haematuria, hypertension, low C3, steroid resistance).
questions.note: Typical nephrotic 1-10 y → steroids without biopsy.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old in relapse of nephrotic syndrome with gross ascites develops fever, diffuse abdominal pain, guarding and rebound tenderness. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explain: Loss of immunoglobulins and complement factors in urine plus ascites predispose to spontaneous bacterial (classically pneumococcal) peritonitis. Renal vein thrombosis presents with flank pain and haematuria.
questions.note: Nephrotic complications: spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, renal vein thrombosis, PE.

questions.stem: An 8-year-old develops cola-coloured urine, hypertension and oedema 2 weeks after a sore throat; C3 is low and C4 normal. Which finding at follow-up would be atypical for the likely diagnosis and prompt renal biopsy?
questions.explain: Post-streptococcal GN (1-2 weeks after pharyngitis, 3-6 weeks after skin infection) has low C3 with normal C4 that normalises by 8 weeks; persistent hypocomplementaemia suggests C3 glomerulopathy/MPGN or lupus. Microscopic haematuria may persist for up to 1-2 years.
questions.note: PSGN: low C3, normal C4, normal by 8 weeks; follows pharyngitis by 1-2 weeks, skin by 3-6 weeks.

questions.stem: On urine dipstick testing for UTI, which result is most specific for bacterial infection?
questions.explain: Nitrites (from Gram-negative nitrate reductase) are specific but insensitive (need urine dwell time - often negative in infants); leucocyte esterase is sensitive but not specific. Culture confirms.
questions.note: UTI: nitrites specific, leucocyte esterase sensitive; nephritic → complement, ASOT.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old has had 6 days of fever, red cracked lips and bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis. He has received no antibiotics. Urine microscopy shows many white cells but the culture is sterile. What is the most likely explanation for the pyuria?
questions.explain: Sterile pyuria has a short differential: partially treated UTI, renal TB, Kawasaki disease and appendicitis. With ≥5 days of fever, oral changes and conjunctivitis, Kawasaki explains it (urethritis-related pyuria).
questions.note: Sterile pyuria: partially treated UTI, renal tuberculosis, Kawasaki disease, appendicitis.

cards.front: Contrast nephrotic and nephritic syndrome.
cards.back: Nephrotic: heavy proteinuria, oedema, albumin <30 g/L, hyperlipidaemia; complications SBP, renal vein thrombosis, PE • Nephritic: haematuria with red cell casts, hypertension, milder proteinuria → complement, ASOT, urgent nephrology.

cards.front: How do you work up proteinuria in a child?
cards.back: Is it real, is it big? • Urinalysis → first-morning urine (excludes orthostatic) → protein:creatinine ratio • Commonest: transient, orthostatic • Nephrotic 1-10 y = minimal change ~90% → steroids without biopsy.

cards.front: Approach to leukocyturia and imaging after UTI.
cards.back: Leukocyturia = UTI until culture negative • Nitrite specific, LE sensitive • Sterile pyuria: partially treated UTI, renal TB, Kawasaki, appendicitis • After UTI: ultrasound → MCUG (VCUG), DMSA.
